name: Zoe Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a cardboard box plant just off the bypass, feeding a die-cutter. That's a big press that stamps flat sheets of cardboard into box shapes, with the folds and the handle holes. I stack the sheets on the feeder, keep an eye on the cuts, knock out the waste bits and stack the finished blanks on pallets. It's dusty and repetitive and my shoulders hurt by Thursday, but I know what I'm doing each day, and I like that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years. I worked in a shoe shop before the kids, then I was home for ten years with Margot and Jules, they're twelve and nine now. When we needed a second wage for the mortgage, this was the only place hiring that didn't want evenings. My husband Luc fixes roads for the council, and we get by, but we never have more than a few weeks' money in the bank. I'm still learning the machine; when they changed the controls to a touch screen last year, I had to write the steps on a card and tape it to the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, good. That suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much. If it came up at lunch I'd say, see, they make a fuss about everything and then it's nothing. I'm not on social media much, a family group chat and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to keep my job and keep doing it the way I do it. I don't want the job to get more exciting, I want it to stay. I took two years to get comfortable with the press, I'd like ten more like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Turn up, do my shift, maybe ask for some more hours if they're going. Keep the card taped to the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd like ten more years like this. What's the best part of a normal week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Friday afternoon, honestly, when the pallets are wrapped and Denise from the next press and I have a coffee from the machine before the bus. That and knowing on Monday the press will be there doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the job worry you now, even in a calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The touch screen still does. Every time they update it, the buttons move. I'm frightened of pressing the wrong thing and ruining a whole run, so I ask Denise. She doesn't mind, but I mind.

S0.say: They make a fuss about everything and then it turns out to be nothing. I'd say that at lunch, not online, because I'm hardly on social media.
S0.think: A flat AI future means I keep my job and keep doing it my way. I don't want the job to get more exciting, I want it to stay.
S0.do: Keeps doing her shifts as usual and asks for extra hours if they come up. Keeps relying on her taped card of steps for the touch screen.
S0.quote: I don't want the job to get more exciting, I want it to stay.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe values stability above everything at work, after taking two years to feel comfortable. Even in the calm picture the touch screen updates bother her. She relies on a colleague for help and feels embarrassed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one I don't like. "Change how they work" is not a phrase I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just how business goes, somebody always finds a cheaper way to make a box. I wouldn't say it's anyone's fault. I'd say we'll have to see what the company does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be one of the first to go. I'm the newest on the presses, I'm slow with screens, and I'm not going to learn computer stuff at forty-three. If the presses get a robot that stacks and a camera that checks, they need one person for three machines, and it won't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back straight away, before anything happens. No holiday next summer, Margot's dance classes would hurt but maybe. I'd keep my head down and work hard so they see I'm reliable. I'd wait and see what they announce, I wouldn't do anything rash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My stomach goes tight. I'd be checking the noticeboard every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn computer stuff at forty-three. If the company offered training in work hours, would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go, because you can't say no. But I'd be useless, I know it, like with the touch screen. I'd go home and cry and then go back the next day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luc that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be careful with money. He'd say "we always are", which is true. Then he'd say his job's safe, roads always need fixing, and I'd feel a bit better and a bit worse, because it means it's me who's the problem.

S1.say: It's just how business goes; someone always finds a cheaper way to make a box. It isn't anyone's fault, and we'll have to see what the company does.
S1.think: I think I'd be one of the first to go: newest, slow with screens and not about to learn computer stuff at forty-three. If one person can run three presses, it won't be me.
S1.do: Cuts back straight away by dropping next summer's holiday and maybe her daughter's dance classes. Keeps her head down to look reliable and waits for the company's announcement before doing anything.
S1.feel: Tight in the stomach, checking the noticeboard every morning.
S1.quote: I'd go home and cry and then go back the next day.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe doesn't blame anyone; she treats it like weather. Her resistance to new tech isn't stubbornness so much as fear of looking useless. Luc's job security comforts her and also makes her feel she's the weak point in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. That's not… No.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably that nobody saw it coming and nobody knows what to do. I'd ask people at work if they'd heard anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be finished, I think. The press is the only thing I've learned in ten years. If a robot can do every job, I can't even go back to the shoe shop, because that'll be robots too. And if Luc's roads go to robots as well, we've got a few weeks and then nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything, food shopping down to the basics, no car if we could manage. I'd go to the job centre straight away and take whatever is going, cleaning, anything. I'd ask my mum if we could move in with her if it got bad, she's got the house in the village. I'd go to the council to ask what help there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I can't breathe. I'd be awake all night. I'd look at the kids and not know what to tell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask your mum about moving in. What would that mean for the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: New school, forty minutes away, and no friends. Margot would hate me. Jules would be fine after a week, he's like that. But it would be a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier it's nobody's fault. Do you still feel that here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe somebody should have stopped it, the government or somebody. But I wouldn't know who. I'm not a political person, I'd just want someone to tell me what to do.

S2.say: Nobody saw it coming and nobody knows what to do. I'd just ask the others at the plant if they had heard anything at all.
S2.think: I'd be finished, because the press is the only thing I've learned in ten years and even the shoe shop would be robots. If Luc's roads go too, we've got a few weeks and then nothing.
S2.do: Cuts everything down to basic food and maybe the car, and goes straight to the job centre to take any work such as cleaning. Asks the council for help and her mother about moving into her village house if it gets bad.
S2.feel: Can't breathe, sleepless, unsure what to tell her kids.
S2.quote: I'm not a political person, I'd just want someone to tell me what to do.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves Zoe with no plan beyond cutting back, any job and family. Her pragmatic "nobody's fault" view wobbles but she can't name anyone to blame. She's looking for guidance more than a cause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast. But not two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's some time, so let's see what the government and the companies come up with. Somebody must have a plan. I'd probably say that at lunch and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still ends with me without a job, I think. Five years just means I see it coming. I'm not going to become a programmer. But maybe the kids are a bit older, Margot would be seventeen, she could have a weekend job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving whatever we can, even a little, and we'd stop the extras now, not later. I'd keep working hard at the press, so I'm one of the last. I'd watch what happens and maybe look for something else in year three or four, but I don't know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, slowly. Like when the doctor says come back in a few months and we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe look for something else in year three or four. Why not sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got a job now, and leaving a job when you've got one is mad. And I don't know what I'd look for. Every job I can think of would be the same in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which extras would stop first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaway on Saturdays, the kids' magazine subscriptions, my hair. I go every eight weeks, I'd go every four months. Luc would grumble about the takeaway.

S3.say: There's some time, so let's see what the government and the companies come up with. Somebody must have a plan.
S3.think: It still ends with me out of a job; five years just means I see it coming. I won't become a programmer, but the kids would be older and Margot could get a weekend job.
S3.do: Saves whatever she can and stops extras like Saturday takeaways and haircuts now. Works hard to be among the last kept, and might look for other work in year three or four.
S3.feel: Slowly building fear, like waiting on a doctor's follow-up.
S3.quote: Like when the doctor says come back in a few months and we'll see.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't open new options for Zoe; it gives her time to save and brace. She sees no target job worth moving to, because she expects every job to go eventually. Her trust that "somebody must have a plan" is how she copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. I'd be fifty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, plenty of time for things to be sorted out. You can't worry about everything ten years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is better for us. The kids would be grown, the mortgage would be smaller. I'd still lose my job in the end, but at fifty-three it's nearly retirement anyway, maybe there'd be something for people my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, put a bit away each month, tell the kids to study something useful. I'd still not go on courses or learn the computer stuff, I'd just do my job well and see. Maybe nearer the time I'd think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried. But I can put it away in a drawer, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fifty-three is nearly retirement. Is it, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really, the pension age is much later. I said it because it's what I'd like. I'd be twelve years short at least. That's the bit I'd put in the drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Margot and Jules to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where they look after people, like nursing, or something with the government, like Luc. Steady things. Not anything you do on a computer, if the computer is doing it all.

S4.say: Ten years is a long way off and there's plenty of time to sort things out. You can't worry about everything a decade ahead.
S4.think: Ten years is better for us, with the kids grown and the mortgage smaller. I'd still lose my job and I'd be about twelve years short of the pension, but I'd rather not think about that.
S4.do: Keeps working and puts a little away each month, and tells her kids to study steady, people-focused work. Avoids courses and computer skills and plans to rethink nearer the time.
S4.feel: A little worried, but able to put it out of mind most days.
S4.quote: I said it because it's what I'd like. I'd be twelve years short at least. That's the bit I'd put in the drawer.
S4.fieldNote: Her public line is relaxed, but the follow-up showed the gap: she called fifty-three "nearly retirement" and then admitted she'd be twelve years short. Ten years lets her avoid the issue rather than prepare for it. Her advice to her children is to seek steady, caring or public jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by far. What would help is someone telling us what to do, clearly. A person at the job centre who knows, and money coming in while we work it out, so we don't lose the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how people feel about being slow. I'm not stupid, I'm just slow with screens. Nobody asks that, they just say "reskill".

headlineQuote: I'm not stupid, I'm just slow with screens. Nobody asks that, they just say "reskill".
portrait: Zoe is forty-three and has fed a die-cutter at a cardboard box plant for two years, after ten years at home raising her children. She wants her job to stay the same, keeps a card of touch-screen steps taped to her press, and won't use AI tools or seek out courses. She's pragmatic and doesn't blame anyone, treating change like weather, but she wants clear guidance when it comes. Calm in the flat scenario, she's panicked by fast AGI and sees ten years mostly as time to put the worry in a drawer.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the press is the only thing she's learned and every fallback job would go too.
whatWouldHelp: Someone at the job centre telling her clearly what to do, and money coming in while she works it out so they don't lose the house.
